items.readable_text:
Content:
The remainder theorem states that for any polynomial [MATH: p(x)] and number [MATH: c,] when we divide [MATH: p(x)] by [MATH: (x-c),] the remainder is equal to [MATH: p(c).]

Content:
For example, consider the polynomial [MATH: p(x)=4x^3-5x^2-7x+3] and the number [MATH: c={\color{red}{2}}.] First, let's divide [MATH: p(x)] by [MATH: (x-{\color{red}{2}})] using synthetic division:

Content:
| | [MATH: x^3] | [MATH: x^2] | [MATH: x^1] | [MATH: x^0] |
| [MATH: \color{red}2] | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: -5] | [MATH: -7] | [MATH: 3] |
| | [MATH: \color{gray}\downarrow] | [MATH: 8] | [MATH: 6] | [MATH: -2] |
| | [MATH: 4] | [MATH: 3] | [MATH: -1] | [MATH: 1] |

Content:
We get a remainder of [MATH: {\color{blue}1}.] Indeed, when we work out [MATH: p({\color{red}2}),] we also get a result of [MATH: {\color{blue}1},] just like the remainder theorem guarantees:

Content:
[MATH: p(2)|= 4(2)^{3} − 5(2)^{2} − 7(2) + 3; = 32 − 20 − 14 + 3; = 1✓]

Content:
To understand why this happens, notice that we can use the result of the synthetic division to rewrite [MATH: p(x)] as

Content:
[MATH: p(x) = (4x^2+3x-1)(x-2)+{\color{blue}{1}}.]

Content:
When we substitute [MATH: x={\color{red}{2}}] into the above, we see that the [MATH: (x-2)] factor turns to [MATH: 0,] thereby eliminating the quotient [MATH: (4x^2+3x-1)] and leaving only the remainder of [MATH: {\color{blue}{1}}\mathbin{:}]

Content:
[MATH: p(2)|= (4 ⋅ 2^{2} + 3 ⋅ 2 − 1)(2 − 2) + 1; = (4 ⋅ 2^{2} + 3 ⋅ 2 − 1)(0) + 1; = 0 + 1; = 1✓]

Content:
The remainder theorem remains valid even if we substitute [MATH: (x-c)] with [MATH: k(x-c),] as long as [MATH: k] is a non-zero real number. Let's look at an example.

So, when [MATH: p(x)] is divided by [MATH: 3\left(x-\dfrac23\right),] the remainder is [MATH: 2.]

sections.normalized_html:
The remainder theorem states that when [MATH: q(x)] is divided by [MATH: (x+3),] the remainder equals [MATH: q(-3).] Since we're told that the remainder is [MATH: -5,] then, we must have [MATH: q(-3)=-5.]

Evaluating [MATH: q(-3)] directly gives [MATH: q(− 3)|= 2(− 3)^{3} + 3(− 3)^{2} − 5(− 3) + c; = − 54 + 27 + 15 + c; = − 12 + c,]

which means that

[MATH: -5 = -12 + c.]

Solving for [MATH: c] in the equation above, we find that [MATH: c=7.]

sections.normalized_html: Suppose [MATH: f(x) = ax^3 +bx^2 -11x -2] has a factor of [MATH: (x-2)] and remainder of [MATH: -8] when divided by [MATH: (x-1).] Find the values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b.]
sections.readable_text: Suppose [MATH: f(x) = ax^3 +bx^2 -11x -2] has a factor of [MATH: (x-2)] and remainder of [MATH: -8] when divided by [MATH: (x-1).] Find the values of [MATH: a] and [MATH: b.]

sections.normalized_html:
Since [MATH: (x-2)] is a factor of [MATH: f(x)], it must divide into [MATH: f(x)] with no remainder. In other words, when [MATH: f(x)] is divided by [MATH: (x-2),] the remainder is [MATH: 0.] It follows from the remainder theorem that

[MATH: 0|= f(2); = a(2)^{3} + b(2)^{2} − 11(2) − 2; = 8a + 4b − 24.]

Likewise, since we're told that the remainder is [MATH: -8] when [MATH: f(x)] is divided by [MATH: (x-1),] it follows from the remainder theorem that

[MATH: − 8|= f(1); = a(1)^{3} + b(1)^{2} − 11(1) − 2; = a + b − 13.]

We now have the system of equations [MATH: {0 = 8a + 4b − 24; − 8 = a + b − 13.]

Simplifying each equation, we get

[MATH: {2a + b = 6; a + b = 5.]

To eliminate [MATH: b,] we subtract the equations and get

[MATH: 2|a + b|= 6; −|a + b|= 5; a|= 1.]

Finally, we substitute [MATH: a=1] into [MATH: a+b=5] to find [MATH: b=4.]

Therefore, our final solution is [MATH: (a,b) = (1,4).]

[MATH: − 8|= f(1); = a(1)^{3} + b(1)^{2} − 11(1) − 2; = a + b − 13.]

We now have the system of equations
[MATH: {0 = 8a + 4b − 24; − 8 = a + b − 13.]
